title: Trump Orders Curbs on Critical Minerals Scrap Exports to Counter China's Dominance
excerpt: The presidential order empowers the Commerce Department to block e-waste exports, targeting tungsten and battery black mass to boost domestic recycling and reduce reliance on Chinese mineral supply chains.
body:
• President Trump signed an order allowing the Commerce Department to block exports of e-waste containing critical minerals, targeting tungsten and battery "black mass."
  • The U.S. exports roughly 33,000 metric tons of e-waste per month, much of it rich in lithium and other recyclable minerals.
  • The move follows a broader push to restrict defense contractors from sourcing critical minerals from China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea by January 2027.
  • Domestic recyclers have struggled to compete with foreign buyers who pay above-market rates, with firms like Li-Cycle and Ascend Elements filing for bankruptcy.

President Donald Trump on Thursday signed an order giving federal officials the authority to block exports of old batteries and electronic waste filled with critical minerals, according to two White House officials familiar with the matter. The presidential determination is the latest salvo in Washington's campaign to loosen China's stranglehold on materials vital to national security and advanced manufacturing.

What the Order Does

The order empowers the Commerce Department to issue rules preventing so-called "e-waste" from being shipped overseas — a common practice that has drained the U.S. of recoverable minerals for years. The administration's primary targets are tungsten and shredded battery parts known as "black mass," which contain lithium, cobalt, nickel, and other minerals that domestic recyclers could process, according to Reuters.

The scale of the problem is significant. The U.S. exports nearly 33,000 metric tons of e-waste per month, much of it packed with lithium and other critical minerals that can be recycled, according to data from the Basel Action Network, an environmental watchdog group.

"It's going to take many more years to get the needed infrastructure in the ground to compete."

— Chris Berry, minerals industry analyst and consultant

A Struggling Domestic Recycling Industry

The executive action responds directly to complaints from American recyclers who say they cannot compete with foreign buyers — particularly from China — who pay above-market rates for mineral-rich scrap. That dynamic has been devastating for the domestic recycling sector. Li-Cycle and Ascend Elements, two prominent North American recyclers, both filed for bankruptcy over the past 18 months.

Not all the news is grim. In Oklahoma, Blue Whale Materials and two other firms are building battery recycling operations, part of a patchwork of new investments aimed at keeping mineral-rich waste on American soil.

The Bigger Picture: A January 2027 Deadline

The scrap export restrictions fit into a much larger strategy. Starting January 1, 2027, federal regulations will bar defense contractors from purchasing rare earths, magnets, tungsten, molybdenum, and tantalum from China, Russia, Iran, or North Korea. Trump signed a separate executive order on July 20 making it harder for contractors to obtain waivers to these rules, according to Fastmarkets.

But the gap between ambition and reality remains vast. In 2025, U.S. demand for the most common type of rare earth magnet was roughly 48,000 metric tons while domestic sources supplied just 300 metric tons, according to data from the Arthur D. Little consultancy. U.S. firms are on track to produce 5,000 metric tons by year-end — still a fraction of demand.

The Trump administration launched Project Vault in February, a $12 billion effort to stockpile critical minerals. Officials acknowledged in April that they would initially need to buy minerals from "anywhere in the world," including China — an uncomfortable concession for a president who posted on Truth Social: "ALL FEDERAL AGENCIES MUST BUY AMERICAN — NO EXCUSES!"

Global Context and What's Next

The U.S. is not alone in moving to restrict mineral waste exports. The European Union introduced similar measures, classifying waste lithium-ion batteries and black mass as hazardous from September 2026, effectively preventing exports to non-OECD countries. The EU estimates that recycling rare earth waste could meet 20% of its permanent magnet needs.

China, which controls more than 80% of the global minerals-refining sector, has periodically imposed its own export restrictions on rare earths. The International Energy Agency warned this month that $6.5 trillion of global manufacturing is at risk if Beijing escalates those curbs.

For investors and industries watching critical minerals, the coming months will be pivotal. The Commerce Department must now draft the specific rules governing scrap exports, a process that could take months. Meanwhile, dozens of U.S. mining and processing projects — from MP Materials' magnet facility in Texas to Energy Fuels' rare earth processing in Utah — are racing to scale up before the January 2027 deadline. Whether domestic capacity can match Washington's ambitions remains the central question.
